entries.summary: Any MeshCore radio on the mesh: a companion, repeater, room server or sensor. Each one is identified by its public key, not its name.
entries.detail: Names can change or be shared by more than one node, which is why NodeScope keeps track of nodes by key.

entries.summary: A radio paired with a phone or computer app, used to send and receive messages. Companions don't pass on other people's traffic.
entries.detail: Most people's first node is a companion. To help the mesh reach further, add a repeater.

entries.summary: A fixed radio that rebroadcasts packets so they travel further. Repeaters on roofs, towers and hills are the backbone of the mesh.
entries.detail: A repeater's height and what's around it matter more than its power. Link Profile helps check a site before you install one.

entries.summary: A node that hosts a shared message board. People log in to it, and it keeps messages for anyone who was out of range.
A node that reports readings, such as temperature or battery level, over the mesh.
A radio connected to the internet that reports everything it hears to an analyzer. Everything NodeScope shows comes from observers.
entries.detail: A packet that no observer heard doesn't appear in NodeScope, even if it reached people on the mesh. More observers give a fuller picture.

entries.summary: A short announcement a node broadcasts now and then with its name, type and, if shared, its location. Adverts are how nodes appear on the map.
entries.detail: A node that hasn't sent an advert recently can still be working; it may just be quiet.

entries.summary: The server that collects reports from observers, such as CoreScope or Beacon. NodeScope reads its data from the analyzer you choose in Settings.
Each repeater that passed a packet along. Zero hops means the observer heard the sender directly.
entries.detail: More hops reach further, but every hop adds delay and another chance for the packet to be lost.

entries.summary: The chain of repeaters a packet travelled through to reach an observer. Different observers can hear the same packet over different routes.
entries.detail: NodeScope names each route after the observer that heard it.

entries.summary: A repeater in a route that can't be identified. Routes only carry a short part of each repeater's key, and sometimes no known node matches, or more than one does.
A flood packet is repeated by every repeater that hears it, to find the way. A direct packet follows a route that's already known, through specific repeaters.
entries.detail: Messages usually start as floods. Once a route is learned, later messages to the same node can go direct, which is quieter for the mesh.

entries.summary: One observer hearing one packet. A packet heard by five observers has five observations.
The observers that received this exact route, with the signal they heard it at.
Observers that heard the same packet at an earlier point on its route, before it had made all of its hops.
Signal-to-noise ratio, in dB: how far the signal stood above the background noise. Higher is better, and LoRa can still decode signals a little below zero.
entries.detail: Roughly: above 5 dB is solid, around 0 dB is workable, and well below zero is at the edge of what the radio can decode.

entries.summary: Received signal strength, in dBm. Closer to zero is stronger: −60 dBm is strong, −120 dBm is very weak.
entries.detail: RSSI counts noise as well as signal, so a strong RSSI with a poor SNR usually means a noisy location.

entries.summary: A group chat on the mesh. Messages are encrypted with the channel's key, so only people with the key can read them.
entries.detail: The Public channel uses a key everyone knows, so anyone can read it. Never share anything private there.

entries.summary: An area code, often an airport code such as AUS, that observers are tagged with. Choosing a region shows only traffic heard in that area.
entries.detail: Region groups combine several nearby regions into one choice.

entries.summary: When any observer last received something from this node. It doesn't tell you whether the node is on right now.
entries.detail: A node out of range of every observer can be working fine and still look quiet.

entries.summary: Whether a straight line between the two antennas clears the ground in between. It's necessary for a good link, but not enough on its own.
The football-shaped space around the line of sight that the radio signal fills. Hills that intrude into it weaken the link even when the line of sight is clear.
entries.detail: A common rule of thumb is to keep at least 60% of the zone clear. Link Profile shades the zone on its terrain chart.

entries.summary: How much of the Fresnel zone stays clear of terrain along the path. On the map and chart, green is clear, orange is marginal and red is obstructed.
How many dB the predicted signal exceeds what the receiver needs. Positive means the link should work on paper; 10 dB or more leaves room for fading.
entries.detail: It's an estimate from terrain alone. Buildings, trees and interference aren't included, so treat a small margin with caution.
